title: TLSRPT (RFC 8460) failure reporting for MTA-STS and DANE
description:
## What

RFC 8460 TLS Reporting. A recipient domain publishes a reporting endpoint; senders send it daily JSON summaries of TLS negotiation and policy-validation failures.

Not in scope for the MTA-STS work and never claimed: it is a separate RFC. Filed because the hooks now exist and because it is the half of MTA-STS deployment that makes `testing` mode useful.

## Why it matters more than it sounds

`mode: testing` exists so a domain can deploy MTA-STS and find out what would have broken BEFORE enforcing. Without a sender population that reports, testing mode tells the domain nothing -- it is just a policy that does not apply. §5: "Sending MTAs that also implement the TLSRPT specification send a report indicating policy application failures (as long as TLSRPT is also implemented by the recipient domain); in any case, messages may be delivered as though there were no MTA-STS validation failure."

So a sender that implements MTA-STS without TLSRPT is a free rider on the domains that do: it gets the protection and contributes nothing to anyone else's rollout.

## The hooks already exist

PolicyOutcome::is_validation_failure is true for BOTH FailedEnforce and FailedTesting, which is exactly the reportable set -- the distinction testing mode exists to create. There is a test asserting the two predicates disagree precisely on testing, so that surface is already pinned.

SmtpTransportSecurity::Forbidden carries SmtpTransportDenial, which says whether DANE or MTA-STS refused. RFC 8460 reports on both mechanisms, so that distinction is already the right shape.

## Pieces

TXT DISCOVERY. `_smtp._tls.<domain>` TXT, `v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:...` or `rua=https://...`. Same shape as _mta-sts, so pkix-mta-sts-resolver's lookup is the obvious model; whether it belongs in that crate or its own is part of this work.

REPORT AGGREGATION. Per (policy domain, reporting day) counts by failure type. §4.4 defines the result types: starttls-not-supported, certificate-host-mismatch, certificate-expired, certificate-not-trusted, validation-failure, tlsa-invalid, dnssec-invalid, dane-required, sts-policy-fetch-error, sts-policy-invalid, sts-webpki-invalid. Mapping FetchError and SmtpDaneFailure onto those is most of the design.

REPORT SERIALISATION. §4 JSON, gzipped, §5.1 filename convention.

DELIVERY. §3 says SMTP or HTTPS POST. The SMTP path means sending mail from inside a mail library, which is a dependency question worth deciding deliberately.

## The thing to be careful about

A report says which of a domain's MX hosts failed TLS for which sender. That is operational detail about a third party, sent to an address that third party nominated in unsigned DNS. §7 covers it. Worth deciding what is omitted rather than reporting everything available, and worth not treating the rua address as trusted just because it came from the domain it describes.

## Acceptance

[ ] Decide scope: discovery + aggregation + serialisation, with delivery left to the caller, or all four
[ ] `_smtp._tls` TXT discovery with the rua endpoints parsed, and a decision recorded on which crate it lives in
[ ] A mapping from FetchError, SmtpDaneFailure and PolicyOutcome onto §4.4's result types, with the unmapped cases named
[ ] §4 JSON serialisation with a round-trip test against the RFC's own example report
[ ] Document what is deliberately omitted from a report and why (§7)
[ ] A test that a `testing`-mode failure is reported AND delivered, since that pairing is the whole point of the mode
close_reason:
DONE 2026-11-25. pkix-tlsrpt 0.1.0, no_std. 56 tests; 2259 workspace-wide, no failures.

## Scope decision, which the bead asked for

SHIPPED: §3 _smtp._tls record, §4.4 report schema with serde, §4.3 result types, §5.1 filename, §4.5 policy-string encoding, and classification of this workspace's failures into §4.3's vocabulary.

EXCLUDED, with reasons rather than left undone:

  delivery (mailto)  -- MUST carry a DKIM signature by the reporting domain
                        (§3), without l=, and an unsigned report MUST be
                        ignored by the recipient. That is a mail library and a
                        signing key inside a PKI library, and sending one
                        unsigned is wasted work. Also §5.3: a sender MUST NOT
                        honor its own MTA-STS or DANE failures when delivering
                        a report -- it must mail a report about a domain's
                        broken TLS to that domain, possibly in the clear.
                        That is MTA policy, not PKI.
  delivery (https)   -- a POST a caller with an HTTP client writes in a line.
                        §3 even permits ignoring certificate errors when
                        submitting, since refusing to deliver over a cert
                        problem would suppress the reports most worth sending.
  compression (§5.2) -- needs a gzip dependency the crate does not otherwise
                        want. ReportFilename::extension already distinguishes
                        json from json.gz, and GZIP_MEDIA_TYPE is exported.
  aggregation        -- a sender knows its own delivery attempts; nothing here
                        should hold a day of them.

## The gap worth remembering

sts-webpki-invalid IS NEVER PRODUCED, and that is deliberate.

§4.3.2.2 defines it as "the MTA-STS Policy could not be authenticated using PKIX validation" -- the most security-relevant thing a report can say about MTA-STS, because the HTTPS certificate is the policy's ONLY authentication.

But pkix_mta_sts_http::FetchError::Transport carries both "the certificate did not validate" and "the connection was refused" as one opaque string, because ureq and reqwest report them as incompatible types. Classifying Transport as sts-webpki-invalid would tell a domain its certificate is broken whenever its policy host is merely down -- worse than imprecise, because an operator would chase a certificate that is fine.

So it maps to sts-policy-fetch-error and the stronger claim is left unmade. There is a TEST asserting no FetchError maps to sts-webpki-invalid, so whoever adds a TLS-specific FetchError variant sees it fail and updates the mapping. Filed separately.

## A privacy rule that needed enforcing, not documenting

A report says which of a domain's MX hosts failed TLS, how, and from which sending IP -- operational detail about a third party, sent to an address that third party nominated in UNSIGNED DNS (§3 carries no authentication, exactly like _mta-sts). §7 covers it.

failure-reason-code is the only free-text field in the schema, so it is where a sender would most easily disregard §7. The classifiers therefore emit a CLASSIFICATION (no-trusted-path, http-status-404) and never the error's own text, which can carry a URL or an internal hostname. There is a test that puts an internal URL in the error and asserts it does not reach the code.

## §4.5's trap, called out by the RFC itself

"where there are multiple mx values, they must be listed as separate mx elements in the policy array rather than as a single nested mx sub-array"

The obvious encoding groups them. sts_policy_string produces the flat form and a test counts the elements rather than only comparing the array.

## Two wrong test premises, again

1470013207 is 01:00:07 UTC, not 00:20:07. Checked against date(1) rather than argued about. The implementation was right.

Asserting no underscore appears anywhere in the serialised JSON was too crude: policy-string legitimately contains the MTA-STS policy's own `max_age:` line, which is content, not a field name. The test now walks the JSON keys.

That is the sixth and seventh wrong premise in this stretch of work. The pattern is consistent -- the implementation was right both times -- and the lesson holds: verify against an independent source (date(1), the RFC text, openssl) rather than against what I expect.

## Small things

rfc3339_utc is hand-written (Hinnant's civil_from_days) rather than a date dependency: the crate needs exactly one format and owes nothing to time zones or leap seconds. Tested on 2000 and 2024 being leap years, 2100 NOT being one (the century rule), and both February and December boundaries.

Unknown result-type and policy-type values round-trip byte-identical rather than being rejected, because §4.3 expects the list to grow.

Added _typos.toml for `helo` -- §4.4's field name is receiving-mx-helo and HELO is the SMTP command, so "correcting" it would change the wire format. The five crates added across the MTA-STS work are now in the typos CI gate, all clean.

## Acceptance

[x] Decide scope -- above
[x] _smtp._tls TXT discovery with the rua endpoints parsed, and a decision recorded on which crate it lives in (its own, since TLSRPT reports on DANE too and should not require MTA-STS)
[x] A mapping from FetchError, SmtpDaneFailure and PolicyOutcome onto §4.4's result types, with the unmapped cases named
[x] §4 JSON serialisation with a round-trip test against the RFC's own example report
[x] Document what is deliberately omitted from a report and why (§7)
[x] A test that a testing-mode failure is reported AND delivered -- the classify side asserts a FailedTesting outcome yields certificate-host-mismatch, and pkix-chain's existing precedence suite asserts the same outcome permits delivery
